newsitem.title: USA: Second-quarter worker compensation points to US growth.
newsitem.headline: Second-quarter worker compensation points to US growth.

text.p: Workers' pay and benefits grew at a steady pace in the second quarter, helping to buoy consumer confidence and pointing to vigorous economic growth in the third quarter, reports released Tuesday showed.
The Labour Department's Employment Cost Index rose by 0.8 percent last quarter after increasing by 0.6 percent in the first quarter, the department said.
Wages and salaries rose 0.8 percent, a touch below their 0.9 percent increase in the first three months of 1997.
A rebound in benefits costs, however, helped offset the slower wage growth and lift the overall index. Costs of employee benefits climbed 0.6 percent vs. an 0.1 percent gain in the first quarter.
Despite a slight slip from the previous quarter, wages and salaries advanced at a healthy rate between April and June.

"Real wages are rising fairly nicely and that is one of the things that contributes to consumers being able to spend," said Peter Kretzmer, senior economist at NationsBanc Capital Markets Inc. in New York.
Up 3.2 percent in the year ended June 30, American workers' pay gains have outstripped the 2.3 percent advance in consumer inflation during the same period, resulting in greater purchasing power.

While workers might prefer to see larger annual pay increases, the combination of modest compensation growth and low inflation offers long-run economic stability, said Oscar Gonzalez, an economist at John Hancock Mutual Life Insurance in Boston.

"There is an illusion here that's very hard to get rid of that you want to see your salary increase in the 4.0 to 5.0 percent range," Gonzalez said. "Even if inflation is eating away some of that nominal gain, you still feel better off."

The benefits segment of the compensation report showed that moderate growth in those costs continued to offset faster increases in employee pay. Economists have watched benefits costs closely in recent quarters to gauge whether the efficiencies of managed health care were still limiting overall compensation growth.
"In the past, we've seen that HMOs (health maintenance organisations) were able to squeeze a lot of the costs out of the system, but eventually they came back," Gonzalez said.
A separate report on Tuesday showed that consumers remained confident about their jobs and finances in the first month of the third quarter.
The Conference Board's consumer confidence index fell to 126.5 in July from 129.9 in June but remained at a level that signals solid economic growth, the business research group said.
Asked by reporters whether the downturn suggested consumer confidence had peaked, Conference Board senior economist Ken Goldstein said, "not necessarily."
The confidence index tends to reflect consumers' pay gains, the health of the labour market and the longevitiy of economic expansion, NationsBanc's Kretzmer said.
"We're at very high levels," Kretzmer said, adding that the small drop in the index level did not seem significant.
